### Problem: Minimum falling path sum II {#sec-gd-p2-fall}

::: {.p-statement}
Given an $n \times n$ integer matrix, choose one element from every row so that no two elements chosen in adjacent rows are in the same column. Return the minimum possible sum.

$1 \le n \le 200$ and every entry is between $-99$ and $99$. On $[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]$ the answer is 13, the cells $1, 5, 7$. On $[[7]]$ the answer is 7.

Source: [LC 1289 · Minimum Falling Path Sum II](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-falling-path-sum-ii/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Read the chosen cells from top to bottom. From column $c'$ in the previous row the next choice may be any column except $c'$. So $P(r, c)$ is the whole previous row except column $c$: $n - 1$ predecessors, not the three of an ordinary falling path. Every move goes down one row, so row-by-row order is valid, and the order inside a row does not matter.

"Take the smallest allowed cell of each row" loses. On $[[1, 2], [1, 10]]$ it takes the 1 in column 0 and is then forced to take 10: total 11. The optimum is $2 + 1 = 3$. A slightly worse first choice keeps the cheap column free.

If the best choice for rows $0..r$ ends in column $c$, its rows $0..r-1$ are a best choice ending in some other column. The cells of one row share almost the same predecessors. The minimum of the previous row, the column that holds it, and the second minimum answer "best except column $c$" in $O(1)$. A second copy of the minimum is a legal other column. This is the same summary as Vacation (@sec-dpi-p4-vacation), with $n$ activities instead of three, and a minimum instead of a maximum.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $dp[r][c]$ = minimum sum of a valid choice for rows $0..r$ that uses column $c$ in row $r$.
- **Transition.** $dp[r][c] = g[r][c] + \min_{c' \ne c} dp[r-1][c']$.
- **Base.** $dp[0][c] = g[0][c]$. **Answer.** $\min_c dp[n-1][c]$. **Order.** Row by row.
- **Cost.** The direct table is $O(n^3)$, fine at $n = 200$. Best and second best are $O(n^2)$ time. The summary of the newest row can be kept in three integers, so the table itself need not be stored. Sums stay inside $\pm 200 \cdot 99$.
:::

::: {#fig-gd-fall}

The table for sample 1. Row 1 has a tie at 6, so the second minimum is also 6, and column 0 of the last row may use it: $7 + 6 = 13$.

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
`f(r, c)` is the minimum sum of rows `r` through the end when row `r` uses column `c`. Try every other column of the next row. The last row is just the cell itself. The answer is the best column of row 0.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("fall", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "13"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def fall_rec(g):
    n = len(g)

    def f(r, c):
        if r == n - 1:
            return g[r][c]
        best = min(f(r + 1, d) for d in range(n) if d != c)
        return g[r][c] + best

    return min(f(0, c) for c in range(n))
```

##### C++

```cpp
int fallRec(int r, int c, const vector<vector<int>>& g) {
    int n = g.size();
    if (r == n - 1) return g[r][c];
    int best = 2000000000;
    for (int d = 0; d < n; ++d)
        if (d != c) best = min(best, fallRec(r + 1, d, g));
    return g[r][c] + best;
}
int fallRecAll(const vector<vector<int>>& g) {
    int n = g.size(), ans = 2000000000;
    for (int c = 0; c < n; ++c) ans = min(ans, fallRec(0, c, g));
    return ans;
}
```
:::

#### Memo

::: {.form-next}
There are $n^2$ calls. The sums can be negative, so $-1$ is not a free sentinel. A separate `None` (or a flag) marks a cell that has not been computed. The body is the previous button.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("fall", "memo")
    assert str(final) == "13"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def fall_memo(g):
    n = len(g)
    memo = [[None] * n for _ in range(n)]

    def f(r, c):
        if memo[r][c] is not None:
            return memo[r][c]
        if r == n - 1:
            memo[r][c] = g[r][c]
            return memo[r][c]
        best = min(f(r + 1, d) for d in range(n) if d != c)
        memo[r][c] = g[r][c] + best
        return memo[r][c]

    return min(f(0, c) for c in range(n))
```

##### C++

```cpp
int fallMemo(int r, int c, const vector<vector<int>>& g, vector<vector<int>>& memo, vector<vector<char>>& done) {
    int n = g.size();
    if (done[r][c]) return memo[r][c];
    if (r == n - 1) { done[r][c] = 1; return memo[r][c] = g[r][c]; }
    int best = 2000000000;
    for (int d = 0; d < n; ++d)
        if (d != c) best = min(best, fallMemo(r + 1, d, g, memo, done));
    done[r][c] = 1;
    return memo[r][c] = g[r][c] + best;
}
```
:::

#### Table

::: {.form-next}
Row 0 is the grid. Every later cell adds the minimum of the previous row outside its own column. The inner scan is $n$ per cell. Nothing inside a row depends on anything else in that row.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("fall", "tab")
    assert str(final) == "13"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def fall_tab(g):
    n = len(g)
    dp = [row[:] for row in g]
    for r in range(1, n):
        for c in range(n):
            best = min(dp[r - 1][d] for d in range(n) if d != c)
            dp[r][c] = g[r][c] + best
    return min(dp[-1])
```

##### C++

```cpp
int fallTab(const vector<vector<int>>& g) {
    int n = g.size();
    vector<vector<int>> dp = g;
    for (int r = 1; r < n; ++r)
        for (int c = 0; c < n; ++c) {
            int best = 2000000000;
            for (int d = 0; d < n; ++d)
                if (d != c) best = min(best, dp[r - 1][d]);
            dp[r][c] = g[r][c] + best;
        }
    return *min_element(dp[n - 1].begin(), dp[n - 1].end());
}
```
:::

#### Best and second best

::: {.form-next}
The inner minimum is the row minimum $m_1$, except in the column $j$ that holds it, where it is the second minimum $m_2$. A duplicate of $m_1$ updates $m_2$, so two equal minima give $m_2 = m_1$. For $n = 1$ the loop over rows never needs $m_2$: there is no previous row. The same three numbers can be rebuilt while the new row is produced, and the row itself thrown away. A virtual row of zeros above row 0 removes the special case.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("fall", "best")
    assert str(final) == "13"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def fall_best(g):
    n = len(g)
    m1, m2, j = 0, 0, -1
    for r in range(n):
        n1, n2, nj = 10**18, 10**18, -1
        for c in range(n):
            v = g[r][c] + (m2 if c == j else m1)
            if v < n1:
                n2, n1, nj = n1, v, c
            elif v < n2:
                n2 = v
        m1, m2, j = n1, n2, nj
    return m1

def fall_distinct(g):
    """Second distinct value. A repeated minimum is treated as if it were not there."""
    n = len(g)
    prev = g[0][:]
    for r in range(1, n):
        m1, m2, j = 10**18, 10**18, -1
        for d, v in enumerate(prev):
            if v < m1:
                m2, m1, j = m1, v, d
            elif v > m1 and v < m2:
                m2 = v
        prev = [g[r][c] + (m2 if c == j else m1) for c in range(n)]
    return min(prev)

def greedy_fall(g):
    n = len(g)
    c = min(range(n), key=lambda j: g[0][j])
    total = g[0][c]
    for r in range(1, n):
        c = min((j for j in range(n) if j != c), key=lambda j: g[r][j])
        total += g[r][c]
    return total

_fall = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
_four = [[2, 1, 3, 4], [6, 5, 4, 1], [7, 8, 2, 9], [3, 1, 5, 2]]
assert fall_rec(_fall) == fall_memo(_fall) == fall_tab(_fall) == fall_best(_fall) == 13
assert fall_rec([[7]]) == fall_memo([[7]]) == fall_tab([[7]]) == fall_best([[7]]) == 7
assert greedy_fall([[1, 2], [1, 10]]) == 11
assert fall_rec([[1, 2], [1, 10]]) == fall_best([[1, 2], [1, 10]]) == 3
assert fall_distinct(_fall) == 14
assert fall_rec(_four) == fall_memo(_four) == fall_tab(_four) == fall_best(_four) == 5
for _ in range(15):
    n = random.randint(1, 3)
    g = [[random.randint(-4, 4) for _c in range(n)] for _r in range(n)]
    assert fall_rec(g) == fall_memo(g) == fall_tab(g) == fall_best(g)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int fallBest(const vector<vector<int>>& g) {
    int n = g.size();
    int m1 = 0, m2 = 0, j = -1;
    for (int r = 0; r < n; ++r) {
        int n1 = 2000000000, n2 = 2000000000, nj = -1;
        for (int c = 0; c < n; ++c) {
            int v = g[r][c] + (c == j ? m2 : m1);
            if (v < n1) { n2 = n1; n1 = v; nj = c; }
            else if (v < n2) n2 = v;
        }
        m1 = n1; m2 = n2; j = nj;
    }
    return m1;
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Recursion** is $O(n \cdot (n-1)^{n-1})$ calls: 21 calls on sample 1, and millions by $n = 8$. **Memoisation** is $O(n^3)$ time, $n^2$ states with an $O(n)$ scan, which is about $8 \cdot 10^6$ steps at $n = 200$. **Table** is the same $O(n^3)$. **Best and second best** is $O(n^2)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory. At $n = 200$ that is about a factor of $n$ less work, and it is optimal: every cell has to be read.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 1$ has no adjacency constraint and no second minimum. The answer is the only cell. A transition that reads $m_2$ overflows.
- Sample 1 ties in row 1: the minimum 6 occurs twice, so $m_2 = 6$, and the last row's column 0 is $7 + 6 = 13$.
- The $4 \times 4$ grid with rows $[2, 1, 3, 4]$, $[6, 5, 4, 1]$, $[7, 8, 2, 9]$, $[3, 1, 5, 2]$ sums to 5, along columns $1, 3, 2, 1$. Column 1 is used twice, in rows that are not adjacent.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Skipping duplicates, `else if (v > m1 && v < m2)`, stores the second distinct value. On sample 1 the row $[6, 6, 7]$ then has $m_2 = 7$, so $dp[2][0] = 14$ and the answer becomes 14. A second copy of the minimum is a legal other column.
- Forgetting $n = 1$. There is no second minimum, and adding a cell to an uninitialised $m_2$ overflows. The loop above never reads $m_2$ when there is no previous row.
- Using $-1$ as "not computed" in the memo. A path sum can be $-1$. Use a separate flag, or a sentinel outside $[-19800, 19800]$.
:::

**Variants.** [AC dp_c · Vacation](https://atcoder.jp/contests/dp/tasks/dp_c) is three activities and a maximum (@sec-dpi-p4-vacation); the same $(m_1, j, m_2)$ summary is the whole transition. [LC 931 · Minimum Falling Path Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-falling-path-sum/){difficulty="Medium"} restricts the next column to $c-1$, $c$, or $c+1$. [LC 1937 · Maximum Number of Points with Cost](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-number-of-points-with-cost/){difficulty="Medium"} allows any column and charges $|c - c'|$; the previous row is summarised by a leftward sweep and a rightward sweep. Columns at least $k$ apart are a prefix minimum and a suffix minimum. Forbidding the column of both of the two previous rows puts that column in the state, $dp[r][c][c']$, which is the extra index of @sec-gd-extra.

::: {.practice}
- A falling path whose consecutive columns differ by at most $k$, in $O(mn)$ independent of $k$. On rows $[5, 1, 9, 8, 7]$, $[2, 9, 9, 9, 3]$, $[9, 8, 1, 7, 9]$, $[4, 6, 9, 9, 2]$ the answers are $20$, $15$, and $6$ for $k = 0, 1, 2$.
- How many minimum falling paths, modulo $10^9+7$, still in $O(n^2)$. Sample 1 is $(13, 1)$. On $[[1, 1, 2], [1, 1, 2], [2, 1, 1]]$ the answer is $(3, 3)$. The summary carries the minimum and its count, plus the next value and its count.
:::
